name: Rafael Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at the laptop around nine, in the box room of our flat, writing short tracks for a music library: thirty-second stings for podcasts, background beds for small online ads. AI tools do a lot of the grunt work now, like splitting stems, rough mixes and chord ideas when I'm stuck. Two or three evenings a month I play keys in a covers band at office parties and the odd wedding.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Badly, some months. The library pays me per track licensed, so I might get ninety in March and six hundred in May. The band is a steady hundred a gig. My partner Ana is a freelance illustrator, so we're two people with lumpy incomes and one shared rent, which makes for a fun spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I wasn't surprised. Online I'd post something like "the tools are good assistants and terrible artists", which is what I already think. In the band group chat I'd send a gif and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a plateau suits me fine. I use the tools every day, and they let me finish four tracks a week instead of two, without the market flooding. My income stays lumpy, but if AI stays a good assistant, my box-room studio turns out twice the music for the same rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep writing four tracks a week and pitch to a second library, a bigger one that pays a small fee up front. I'd try to get the band two more corporate bookings before Christmas. And I'd open a separate account for tax, because last year's bill nearly flattened us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit of a niggle about money, but that's been there since I left college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a niggle. What does that look like in a bad month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a bad month I'm checking the library dashboard three times a day like it's a slot machine. Ana and I once lived on pasta for the last ten days of February. It passes, but it leaves a mark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would be worse off, even in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana, honestly. Illustration got hit by image generators before music did, and even a little automation takes the cheap jobs she relied on. She's had three clients go quiet this year.

say: The tools are **good assistants** and terrible artists.
I'd send a gif to the **band chat** and move on with my week.
think: A plateau suits me: I finish **four tracks** a week instead of two.
The market doesn't **flood**, so my extra output still pays.
do: Pitch to a **second library** that pays a fee up front.
Get the band **two more** corporate bookings before Christmas.
Open a separate **tax account** after last year's bill.
feel: Mostly **fine**, with a **niggle** about money that never quite leaves.
S0.quote: My income stays lumpy, but if AI stays a good assistant, my box-room studio turns out twice the music for the same rent.
fieldNote: He's one of the few who'd do **better** in AI Plateau, thanks to AI tools.
His partner Ana's **illustration work** worries him more than his own.
The **lumpy income** shows in stories like ten days of pasta in February.

steps.text: Pitch tracks to a second library that pays fees up front
Use AI stem and mix tools to finish four tracks a week
Open a separate bank account to save for tax

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it straight: library music is the first thing to go, and nobody should pretend otherwise. I'd post about the union's push for a licensing deal, so AI firms pay into a fund for musicians. I'd also say I use these tools, so I'm not anti-tech, I'm anti-theft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, half my income disappears. Podcasts and small ads were always the budget end, and that's exactly where a generator is good enough. I'm the guy who uses AI every day, and I still think AI will eat the library work that pays half my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within six months I'd start selling something the generators can't: custom music with a real conversation behind it, for local businesses and theatre companies. I'd learn the new tools properly, maybe build a setup that makes adaptive music for games, and charge for setting it up. I'd also join the union's licensing campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but weirdly energised. Like I'm on a moving walkway and I can either run or fall over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell custom music to local businesses. Are there enough of those nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, that's the problem. There are maybe three theatre companies within an hour and one indie game studio. So most of it would have to be online, competing with everyone else doing the same pivot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new monitor speakers I wanted, about four hundred. Then streaming subscriptions, then we'd stop driving to Ana's parents every month. Rent and the laptop are untouchable; the laptop is the business.

say: **Library music** is the first thing to go, and nobody should pretend otherwise.
I'm not anti-tech, I'm **anti-theft**, so AI firms should pay into a fund.
think: **Half my income** disappears when generators cover podcasts and small ads.
Using AI every day doesn't **protect** me from it.
do: Sell **custom music** to local businesses and theatres within six months.
Build an **adaptive music** setup for games and charge for it.
feel: **Alarmed** but oddly **energised**, like running on a moving walkway.

fieldNote: He's the **heaviest AI user** and still predicts losing half his income.
**Few local clients** means his pivot competes online with everyone else's.
His line about being **anti-theft**, not anti-tech, sums up his politics.

steps.text: Offer custom music to the three theatre companies within an hour
Learn adaptive game-music tools and sell setups to an indie studio
Join the union's campaign for an AI licensing fund
Cancel streaming subscriptions and monthly drives to Ana's parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a proper safety net, an income for everyone, paid for by taxing the companies that own these systems. I'd say it online, and to anyone at the band's office parties who'd listen. Probably not great for rebookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, all my desk work is gone by 2028: writing, mixing, producing, pitching. What's left is my hands on a keyboard in a room, and that buys me about three years until the robots. My partner Ana and I would both be out of work in the same year, and we share one rent and zero savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Ana and list every hands-on thing we can both do. I'd push the covers band hard for live bookings, because live still works until 2031, and I'd teach keyboard in person to anyone who'd pay. I'd also look at an electrician apprenticeship, which sounds mad, but it's hands-on and paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dizzy. I'm usually the one telling people to try the new thing, and here the new thing is the whole world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd look at an apprenticeship. Wouldn't robots reach that work too, around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I know that. But an apprenticeship pays while you learn, and three years of wages beats three years of nothing. After that, I honestly don't know what anyone does, which is why I keep saying the government has to step in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that we've been broke before and we were fine, which is only half true. Then we'd make the spreadsheet, because that's what we do when we're scared. She'd draw something rude about the AI companies and we'd laugh.

say: This is the moment for an **income for everyone**, paid by taxing AI owners.
I'd say it even at the band's **office parties**, which might cost rebookings.
think: All my **desk work** is gone by 2028, leaving only hands-on playing.

feel: **Dizzy**, because the new thing he usually champions is now the whole world.
S2.quote: My partner Ana and I would both be out of work in the same year, and we share one rent and zero savings.
fieldNote: Two **freelance earners** in exposed jobs make this a household crisis.
He knows robots reach **trades** by 2031 but wants three years of wages.
Even here, his first instinct is a **spreadsheet**, not despair.

steps.text: Book as many live covers-band gigs as possible before 2031
Teach keyboard lessons in person to local pupils
Apply for a paid electrician apprenticeship
Campaign for a public income funded by taxing AI owners

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, and if the government wastes it, that's on them. I'd push for the musicians' fund and money for retraining. Online I'd share my own plan, because people like seeing someone actually do something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be fine for a couple of years and then not. The library work fades from now on, but I'd have time to shift. Five years is enough time to build something new, as long as my partner Ana and I don't spend the first two pretending it isn't coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year building a live-and-teaching business: in-person keyboard lessons, a small rehearsal room shared with two other musicians, and the band. I'd use AI to run the admin, bookings and adverts, so my hours go into rooms with people. I'd try to save two hundred a month, which would be a first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense but focused. More like exam season than a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A rehearsal room costs money. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd split it three ways, about a hundred and twenty each a month, in an old warehouse unit by the ring road. A friend, Kofi, already rents half of one. If it doesn't pay for itself in a year, I'd get out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ana do in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably teach drawing to kids in person, which she's good at and secretly loves. We'd both end up in rooms with children, which is funny for two people who planned careers behind screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should spend it building things people actually own, like co-ops for musicians and artists. I'd probably help start one locally. Online I'd be the annoying optimist again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still lose the library work early, because the thinking tools keep getting better before full AGI. But ten years is long enough to build a living in rooms rather than on screens. With ten years I'm not scared of the robots, I'm scared of running out of rent money while I build the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to get the rehearsal room and lessons solid, and to help set up a small music co-op with five or six local players who share bookings and gear. I'd still use every AI tool going for the boring stuff. And I'd put money into a proper pension, even fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, mostly. There's still a knot about money, but it's a knot I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said running out of rent money. How close are you to that now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three weeks, if both of us stopped earning. That's the honest number. Every plan I've told you depends on there not being a bad month at the wrong time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten years change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana and I would probably get married; we keep putting it off because weddings cost money. With ten years, a small one in her parents' garden starts to sound sensible. It's odd that the end of the world makes me want to plan a party.

say: Ten years is a **gift** for building things people own, like **co-ops**.
I'd be the **annoying optimist** online again, and I'd mean it.
think: I'd still lose the **library work** early, well before full AGI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ana and I would both lose our work in the same year. What would help is a basic income paid for by taxing the companies that own these systems, and some cheap space where musicians can teach and play in person.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want my old job back if I could. I'd take the music without the rent panic over any job, and the rent panic was never the computer's fault.

headlineQuote: I'd take the music without the rent panic over any job, and the rent panic was never the computer's fault.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old producer** who writes library music and plays keys in a covers band.
He shares rent with his partner Ana, a **freelance illustrator**, with about **three weeks** saved.
He uses **AI tools** every day, yet expects them to take the library work first.
He wants **co-ops**, licensing funds and a public income, calling himself anti-theft, not anti-tech.
His plan in every scenario is to move from screens to **in-person** teaching and live playing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he and Ana would lose their work in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** funded by taxing the companies that own AI.
Cheap **shared space** for musicians to teach and play in person.
